<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent ltx_align_center">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Learning Long-Range Dependencies
<br class="ltx_break">with Temporal Predictive Coding</span></p>
</div><span class="ltx_rule" style="width:100%;height:1.0pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span>
<div id="p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:487.8pt;"><span id="p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;">

<div id="p3" class="ltx_para">

</div>
<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Predictive Coding (PC) is a biologically-inspired learning framework characterised by local, parallelisable operations, properties that enable energy-efficient implementation on neuromorphic hardware. Despite this, extending PC effectively to recurrent neural networks (RNNs) has been challenging, particularly for tasks involving long-range temporal dependencies. Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) remains the dominant method for training RNNs, but its non-local computation, lack of spatial parallelism, and requirement to store extensive activation histories results in significant energy consumption. This work introduces a novel method combining Temporal Predictive Coding (tPC) with approximate Real-Time Recurrent Learning (RTRL), enabling effective spatio-temporal credit assignment. Results indicate that the proposed method can closely match the performance of BPTT on both synthetic benchmarks and real-world tasks. On a challenging machine translation task, with a 15-million parameter model, the proposed method achieves a test perplexity of 7.62 (vs. 7.49 for BPTT), marking one of the first applications of tPC to tasks of this scale. These findings demonstrate the potential of this method to learn complex temporal dependencies whilst retaining the local, parallelisable, and flexible properties of the original PC framework, paving the way for more energy-efficient learning systems.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Backpropagation of errors (BP) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rumelhart et al., 1986</a>)</cite> has long served as the dominant algorithm for training artificial neural networks (ANNs), powering breakthroughs in computer vision <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Krizhevsky et al., 2012</a>)</cite>, natural language processing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Devlin et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, and reinforcement learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mnih et al., 2013</a>)</cite>. In recent years, the scale of ANNs has exploded, with networks now containing billions of parameters. Training these models is becoming prohibitively expensive, especially in terms of energy consumption. This has led to growing concerns about the environmental impact and long-term sustainability of the field <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwartz et al., 2019</a>)</cite>, prompting the search for learning algorithms with lower energy demands.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by the efficiency of biological intelligence, neuroscience-inspired alternatives to BP have started to gain traction. The brain is subjected to strict resource constraints, reasoning and learning with a fraction of the energy of its artificial counterparts. Inspired by this, several works have explored the potential of biologically-inspired learning algorithms as a pathway towards more efficient learning systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie and Seung, 2003</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Scellier and Bengio, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. These algorithms suit neuromorphic hardware, which leverages local, parallelisable computation to replicate the low-power design of the brain.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Predictive Coding (PC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rao and Ballard, 1999</a>)</cite> has emerged as a promising neuroscience-inspired alternative to BP that has the potential to address these energy concerns. With roots in theories of cortical function <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mumford, 1991</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mumford, 1992</a>)</cite>, information theory <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Atick, 1991</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Attneave, 1954</a>)</cite>, and ties to variational inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Friston, 2003</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Friston, 2005</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Friston, 2008</a>)</cite>, PC presents a method of credit assignment consisting of local, parallelisable operations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Recent works have demonstrated that parameter updates produced by PC algorithms can approximate those of BP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Whittington and Bogacz, 2017</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Millidge et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and, under certain conditions, match them exactly <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salvatori et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. This suggests PC has the potential to replicate the strong empirical results of BP via purely local computation. When these equivalence constraints are relaxed, PC has been shown to outperform BP in terms of sample efficiency, robustness, and in online scenarios <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Song et al., 2024</a>)</cite> with recent work demonstrating PC-derived gradients approximate higher-order updates <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mali et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Despite these promising results, much of the PC literature focuses on static, non-temporal data. Although works have proposed algorithms for recurrent neural networks (RNNs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ororbia et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Millidge et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang and Rao, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Annabi et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, they have only seen application on small-scale problems. Furthermore, many of them mark a departure from the flexible, generally applicable nature of the original PC framework, requiring hypernetworks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang and Rao, 2024</a>)</cite> or complex connectivity structures <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ororbia et al., 2020</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To address this issue, this work investigates for the first time whether PC, when combined with a form of Real-Time Recurrent Learning (see Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Real-Time Recurrent Learning (RTRL) ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>), can effectively capture complex temporal relationships in sequential tasks. In doing so, this work makes the following contributions:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Introduces Temporal Predictive Coding with Real-Time Recurrent Learning (tPC RTRL), an algorithm that enables spatio-temporal credit assignment in RNNs whilst retaining the local and parallelisable properties of PC.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Demonstrates that tPC RTRL can closely match the performance of BPTT across both small-scale synthetic tasks and larger real-world datasets, including language modelling on WikiText-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merity et al., 2017</a>)</cite> and translation on an English-French subset of CCMatrix <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwenk et al., 2021</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Provides the first application of PC to train recurrent architectures on large-scale sequence-based tasks, demonstrating the potential of tPC RTRL as a candidate for online learning in energy-efficient edge AI hardware.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Predictive Coding (PC)</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Predictive Coding (PC) is an increasingly popular theory of cortical function. It describes the brain as a hierarchical system, where each layer continuously predicts the activity of the layer below, or at the lowest layer, incoming sensory input. In the short term, these predictions are refined by changes in neural activity, potentially implemented by inhibitory feedback connections in a process which resembles short-term perceptual inference. In the long term, these predictions are improved by changes in synaptic weights, allowing the brain to build an internal model of the environment, a process which reflects learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">When considered from a machine learning perspective, PC yields an algorithm consisting of local, parallelisable operations with both inference and learning rules driven by gradient descent on a single quantity known as the free energy. In practice, neural implementations of PC adopt an Expectation-Maximisation (EM) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dempster et al., 1977</a>)</cite> approach known as Inference Learning (IL) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Whittington and Bogacz, 2017</a>)</cite>. This begins with an iterative inference phase where the free energy is minimised with respect to the model’s internal activations (E-step), before further minimising the free energy, this time with respect to the parameters of the model (M-step). Although this is seen as the standard implementation, other variants of EM, such as incremental EM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Neal and Hinton, 1998</a>)</cite>, can also be used <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Salvatori et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. The following section introduces the concept of free energy for a general hierarchical PC model, before describing how PC can be applied to RNNs in a temporal setting.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Free Energy</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The free energy, <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}</annotation></semantics></math>, for a PC network is defined as:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle D_{\text{KL}}[Q(\mathbf{x}_{1:L};\theta)||P(\mathbf{x}_{1:L}|\mathbf{o};\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1})]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mtext>KL</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>𝐨</mi><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle D_{\text{KL}}[Q(\mathbf{x}_{1:L};\theta)||P(\mathbf{x}_{1:L}|\mathbf{o};\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1})]</annotation></semantics></math></td>

</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where:</p>
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐨</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{o}</annotation></semantics></math> is some observed sensory input.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{1:L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{1:L}</annotation></semantics></math> are the latent variables across layers 1 to <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="Q(\mathbf{x}_{1:L};\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(\mathbf{x}_{1:L};\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> is an approximate posterior over the latent variables, parameterised by <math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="P(\mathbf{x}_{1:L}|\mathbf{o};\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>𝐨</mi><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(\mathbf{x}_{1:L}|\mathbf{o};\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1})</annotation></semantics></math> is the recognition density describing the most likely latent variables given the sensory input and the parameters of the model, <math id="S2.I1.i4.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{KL}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{KL}</annotation></semantics></math> term measures the divergence between the approximate posterior and the true recognition density, which can be interpreted as a measure of how well the inferred latent variables align with the prior beliefs of the model. The log-likelihood term quantifies how well these inferred variables explain the incoming observations under the model. This presents a familiar complexity-accuracy trade-off, where minimising this free energy encourages the model to find a balance between fitting observations with minimal violation of prior beliefs.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">From Free Energy to Local Errors</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Within a PC network, it is assumed that the joint distribution over latent variables and sensory input, where <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}=\mathbf{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>𝐨</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}=\mathbf{o}</annotation></semantics></math>, has the following structure:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle P(\mathbf{x}_{1:L},\mathbf{x}_{0})=P(\mathbf{x}_{L})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle P(\mathbf{x}_{1:L},\mathbf{x}_{0})=P(\mathbf{x}_{L})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\prod_{l=0}^{L-1}P(\mathbf{x}_{l}|\mathbf{x}_{l+1})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∏</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\prod_{l=0}^{L-1}P(\mathbf{x}_{l}|\mathbf{x}_{l+1}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, let <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P(\mathbf{x}_{l}|\mathbf{x}_{l+1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P(\mathbf{x}_{l}|\mathbf{x}_{l+1})</annotation></semantics></math> be a multivariate Gaussian with mean <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> and covariance <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>, such that:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=g_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{l+1};\mathbf{W}_{l})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=g_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{l+1};\mathbf{W}_{l}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> is a deterministic function which takes the latent variables at the layer above, <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{l+1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{l+1}</annotation></semantics></math>, and is parameterised by the weights of the layer, <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>. These functions represent the layer-wise downward predictions typical of PC theory. This gives the network the following structure:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle P(\mathbf{x}_{1:L},\mathbf{x}_{0})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle P(\mathbf{x}_{1:L},\mathbf{x}_{0})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_{L};0,1)\prod_{l=0}^{L-1}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_{l};\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{l})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∏</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_{L};0,1)\prod_{l=0}^{L-1}\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_{l};\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l},\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{l}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="Q(\mathbf{x}_{1:L};\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q(\mathbf{x}_{1:L};\theta)</annotation></semantics></math> factorise via a mean-field approximation into conditionally independent distributions over latent variables at each layer:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle Q(\mathbf{x}_{1:L};\theta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo><mi>θ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle Q(\mathbf{x}_{1:L};\theta)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\prod_{l=0}^{L-1}Q(\mathbf{x}_{l};\theta_{l})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∏</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>θ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\prod_{l=0}^{L-1}Q(\mathbf{x}_{l};\theta_{l}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Now, when modelling these factors with appropriate distributions, either a Gaussian distribution or Dirac delta function, the free energy reduces to a sum of precision-weighted local errors. After dropping constants, this becomes:</p>
<table id="S2.E6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}=\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\left[\ln|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{l}|+\frac{||\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{l}||^{2}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{l}}\right]," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munderover><mo movablelimits="false" rspace="0em">∑</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mfrac><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi>𝚺</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}=\sum_{l=0}^{L-1}\left[\ln|\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{l}|+\frac{||\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{l}||^{2}}{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}_{l}}\right],</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{l}=\mathbf{x}_{l}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{l}=\mathbf{x}_{l}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> is the prediction error at layer <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="l" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>l</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">l</annotation></semantics></math>. In most implementations, the covariances are set to fixed identity matrices and disappear. For a full demonstration of how <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}</annotation></semantics></math> reduces to a sum of local errors, see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Millidge et al. (2021)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This general description defines a generative hierarchical PC network where the highest latent variables, <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{L}</annotation></semantics></math>, are assumed to be drawn from some fixed distribution. For a discriminative PC model, <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{L}</annotation></semantics></math> is assumed to be drawn from some input data generating distribution. This work adopts the discriminative form, taking input data at the highest level and predicting a target output, or label, at <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>. Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Inference Learning Algorithm" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> describes this process in detail.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Temporal Predictive Coding</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Temporal Predictive Coding (tPC) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Millidge et al., 2024</a>)</cite> is a variant of PC which extends the original framework to sequential data and recurrent models. Under this definition, inference should also depend on <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1:L}^{(t-1)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1:L}^{(t-1)}</annotation></semantics></math>, the converged hidden state from the previous time step:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx6" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle P(" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo fence="true" lspace="0em">CLOSE</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle P(</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{1:L}^{(t)},\mathbf{x}_{0}^{(t)},\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1:L}^{(t-1)})=" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{1:L}^{(t)},\mathbf{x}_{0}^{(t)},\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1:L}^{(t-1)})=</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S2.E7"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle P(\mathbf{x}_{L}^{(t)})P(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}_{0}|\mathbf{x}^{(t)}_{1})\prod_{l=1}^{L-1}P(\mathbf{x}_{l}^{(t)}|\mathbf{x}_{l+1}^{(t)},\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{l}^{(t-1)})." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">∏</mo><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover></mstyle><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">|</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle P(\mathbf{x}_{L}^{(t)})P(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}_{0}|\mathbf{x}^{(t)}_{1})\prod_{l=1}^{L-1}P(\mathbf{x}_{l}^{(t)}|\mathbf{x}_{l+1}^{(t)},\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{l}^{(t-1)}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(7)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This yields a hierarchy of Gaussians similar to the static case, but with layer-wise prediction functions <math id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="g_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">g_{l}</annotation></semantics></math> which incorporate this new dependency:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E8"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}^{(t)}=\begin{cases}g_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{l+1}^{(t)};\mathbf{W}_{l})&amp;\text{if }l=0\\
g_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{l+1}^{(t)},\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{l}^{(t-1)};\mathbf{W}_{l})&amp;\text{otherwise}\end{cases}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>otherwise</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}^{(t)}=\begin{cases}g_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{l+1}^{(t)};\mathbf{W}_{l})&amp;\text{if }l=0\\
g_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{l+1}^{(t)},\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{l}^{(t-1)};\mathbf{W}_{l})&amp;\text{otherwise}\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(8)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">The free energy under this definition remains the same sum of local errors. At each time step, the iterative inference process is conducted to find the latents that best explain the sensory input and are consistent with the previous time step’s inferences. The parameters of the network could be updated in an online fashion, or batched through time and applied once the whole sequence has been presented. Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Temporal PC Algorithm" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a> describes the tPC algorithm in full.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Real-Time Recurrent Learning (RTRL)</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Williams and Zipser (1989)</a></cite> were the first to introduce Real-Time Recurrent Learning (RTRL), as an alternative to BPTT for training RNNs. Unlike BPTT, the memory requirement of RTRL is independent of the length of the input sequence, as it does not need to hold the whole unrolled network in memory. Instead, RTRL performs credit assignment by maintaining, and recursively updating, an influence matrix, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{M}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐌</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{M}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math>, which tracks the contribution of each parameter to the current hidden state, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math>. Consider an RNN with a single hidden layer of <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> units with <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> parameters, excluding read-out weights which can be learnt without the need for temporal information. The recursive influence matrix update is given by:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx8" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{M}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐌</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{M}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S2.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(t)}}+\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t-1)}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t-1)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>+</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(t)}}+\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t-1)}}\frac{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t-1)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S2.E9"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\underbrace{\mathbf{\bar{M}}^{(t)}}_{\text{Immediate Influence}}+\underbrace{\mathbf{J}^{(t)}\mathbf{M}^{(t-1)}}_{\text{Historic Influence}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder><munder accentunder="true"><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐌</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>Immediate Influence</mtext></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><msup><mi>𝐉</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐌</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>Historic Influence</mtext></munder></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\underbrace{\mathbf{\bar{M}}^{(t)}}_{\text{Immediate Influence}}+\underbrace{\mathbf{J}^{(t)}\mathbf{M}^{(t-1)}}_{\text{Historic Influence}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(9)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> represents an application of the parameters at <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{\bar{M}}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐌</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{\bar{M}}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the immediate influence of the parameters on the current hidden state and <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{J}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐉</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{J}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the Jacobian of the hidden state transition function. With this matrix maintained, exact gradients with respect to an incoming loss, <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math>, can be computed directly:</p>
<table id="S2.E10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t)}}\mathbf{M}^{(t)}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐌</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{x}^{(t)}}\mathbf{M}^{(t)}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(10)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Although RTRL presents a method of performing spatio-temporal credit assignment with memory requirements that are independent of the input sequence length, it still suffers from memory issues, this time when scaling with network size. The influence matrix typically occupies <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="nP\approx O(n^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">nP\approx O(n^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> memory, making it impractical for large networks. In addition, when considering multi-layer RNNs, each hidden layer is influenced by all of the parameters of the layers below. Therefore, an <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> layer network must maintain <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L(L+1)/2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L(L+1)/2</annotation></semantics></math> influence matrices <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Irie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. BPTT does not suffer from this issue and scales linearly with the number of layers in both time and memory requirements. Recent works have explored methods of reducing the requirements of multi-layer RTRL, demonstrating that some of the benefits of increased network expressability can be obtained if each layer maintains an influence matrix for only its own parameters <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zucchet et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Several works have explored methods of reducing the <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(n^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(n^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> memory requirements of RTRL. This includes approximating the influence matrix via decomposition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mujika et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tallec and Ollivier, 2018</a>)</cite> or introducing sparse approximations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Menick et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Other works have considered the design of recurrent cells which make exact RTRL tractable <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Irie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zucchet et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. These works rely on the idea of element-wise recurrence, where each hidden node is influenced by a distinct subset of its own parameters. This diagonalises the influence matrix, as there are no intra-layer connections to consider.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Methods</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, tPC networks fail to reliably learn long-range temporal relationships in sequential data. In some generative cases, where the next input can be predicted largely from recent context, this limitation is less obvious. However, many applications require the ability to model these types of relationships, especially when information must be aggregated from distant time steps to make accurate predictions. To solve these challenges, this section introduces a form of RTRL-enhanced tPC, subsequently referred to as tPC RTRL.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>RTRL-enhanced tPC</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Under the definition of tPC introduced in Section <a href="#S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" title="Temporal Predictive Coding ‣ 2.1 Predictive Coding (PC) ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>, the parameters are learnt via gradient descent on the free energy at time <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. That is:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx9" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E11"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{W}=-\eta\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}^{(t)}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}}\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(t)}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝝁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝝁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\Delta\mathbf{W}=-\eta\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}^{(t)}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}}\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(t)}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(11)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math> is a parameter learning rate and <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> represents an application of the parameters <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐖</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}</annotation></semantics></math> at time <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>. For readout parameters which do not influence the hidden state, this is sufficient. However, this update rule fails to account for the fact that some parameters influence the free energy not only through their immediate application at the current time step, but also through their historic influence on the evolving hidden state. An update rule which takes this into account is likely to yield better performance when capturing long-range relationships present in data.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Following RTRL, consider a matrix, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{M}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐌</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{M}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math>, which estimates the influence of the parameters on the current hidden state, <math id="S3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math>. Using this, an update which considers the historic influence of the parameters over several time steps can be defined as:</p>
<table id="S3.E12" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta\mathbf{W}=-\eta\left(\underbrace{\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}^{(t)}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}}\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}}{\partial\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t-1)}}\mathbf{M}^{(t-1)}}_{\text{Historic}}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(t)}}}_{\text{Immediate}}\right)" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>𝐖</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝝁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝝁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐌</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>Historic</mtext></munder><mo>+</mo><munder><munder accentunder="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>Immediate</mtext></munder></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta\mathbf{W}=-\eta\left(\underbrace{\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}^{(t)}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}}\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}}{\partial\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t-1)}}\mathbf{M}^{(t-1)}}_{\text{Historic}}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}^{(t)}}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(t)}}}_{\text{Immediate}}\right)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The typical RTRL rule for updating the influence matrix requires calculating the Jacobian of the hidden state transition function, and the immediate influence of the parameters on the current hidden state (Eq. <a href="#S2.E9" title="In 2.2 Real-Time Recurrent Learning (RTRL) ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>). However, in the case of tPC, the hidden state transition is not defined by a feedforward function, but rather an optimisation process. Therefore, the influence matrix update rule must be changed to reflect that the converged hidden state does not necessarily take the value of the predicted hidden state:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx10" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E13"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{M}^{(t)}=\left[\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu^{(t)}}}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(t)}}+\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu^{(t)}}}{\partial\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t-1)}}\mathbf{M}^{(t-1)}\right]_{\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>𝐌</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝝁</mi><mrow><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒕</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>+</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>𝝁</mi><mrow><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>𝒕</mi><mo class="ltx_mathvariant_bold" mathvariant="bold" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mi>𝐌</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝝁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{M}^{(t)}=\left[\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu^{(t)}}}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(t)}}+\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu^{(t)}}}{\partial\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t-1)}}\mathbf{M}^{(t-1)}\right]_{\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">The key difference between this update rule and that of RTRL is that the converged hidden state <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> is substituted for the predicted hidden state <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝝁</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> when updating the influence matrix. At the point of ideal convergence, where <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}=0</annotation></semantics></math>, these two terms are exactly equal, and therefore this update rule becomes exact. In practice, this is almost never the case as there is usually always some internal error present. However, the results in this Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> demonstrate that this approximation is sufficient to allow the model to learn in both small problems and on real-world datasets. The full tPC RTRL algorithm is described in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C tPC RTRL Algorithm" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section demonstrates that tPC RTRL can effectively learn long-range temporal relationships in sequential data, addressing the limitations of the tPC baseline. This will begin by exploring a synthetic sequence copy task, before considering 2 larger real-world datasets: language modelling on WikiText-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merity et al., 2017</a>)</cite> and machine translation on an English-French subset of CCMatrix <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwenk et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. The results of these experiments demonstrate that tPC RTRL can closely match the performance of BPTT, showing its ability to learn long-range temporal relationships.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Copy Task</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For this task, the model is presented with a sequence of digits and required to output the same sequence after a fixed delay. Although the task is simple, the information required to make these predictions is separated from the learning signal by several time steps, making it difficult for models to succeed without the ability to capture long-range dependencies.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18131v1/data/copy_tpc_rtrl.png" id="S4.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:673/190;" width="673" height="190" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Cross-Entropy Loss and Accuracy of BPTT, Spatial BP, tPC and tPC RTRL on the Sequence Copying Task in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Copy Task ‣ 4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>. The Shaded Regions Represent the Standard Deviation of the Results Across 5 Runs.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Setup:</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The input is a sequence of 30 digits sampled uniformly from the integers 1-9, with 0 reserved as a padding token. The target output is the same sequence of digits translated 10 time steps into the future with both sequences padded for a total of 40 time steps. The network architecture for all models considered is a many-to-many RNN with a single hidden layer of 128 units and <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">tanh</span> nonlinearities.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Four models are trained on this task, one with each learning algorithm considered in this work: BPTT, spatial BP, tPC, and tPC RTRL. The BPTT model is trained using the standard BPTT algorithm, unrolling the network across all time steps of the sequence to aggregate the influence of all historic applications of the network parameters. The spatial BP model is trained using BP without temporal information. This means that for each incoming loss, only the most recent application of the network parameters is included in the compute graph. The tPC and tPC RTRL models are trained using the algorithms described in Sections <a href="#S2.SS1.SSS0.Px3" title="Temporal Predictive Coding ‣ 2.1 Predictive Coding (PC) ‣ 2 Background" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> and <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 RTRL-enhanced tPC ‣ 3 Methods" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, respectively. Both BP-based models use a cross-entropy loss, whilst the PC-based models use a squared-error loss function for internal energy and a cross-entropy loss function for output energy as in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pinchetti et al. (2022)</a></cite>. Furthermore, both use an inference learning rate of 0.9 and complete 4 inference iterations per time step. All models are trained with a batch size of 16 and evaluated on 200 randomly generated test samples every 16 batches. For full details of the experimental setup, see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS1" title="D.1 Sequence Copying Task ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results:</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The results of this experiment are shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 4.1 Copy Task ‣ 4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. First, it is clear that the baseline tPC and spatial BP training methods are not successful in this task, clearly demonstrating the limitations of tPC and highlighting the need for an improved method of capturing relationships of this kind. On the other hand, BPTT and tPC RTRL handle the task with ease, quickly reaching near perfect accuracy, with both methods exhibiting similar stability and speed of convergence. Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Results: ‣ 4.1 Copy Task ‣ 4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports the validation loss and accuracy of BPTT and tPC RTRL, averaged over 5 runs, providing further evidence that the proposed method closely matches the performance of BPTT.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>The Validation Loss and Accuracy of tPC RTRL and BPTT on the Sequence Copying Task.
