</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>WikiText-2</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The results seen on the previous task highlight that tPC RTRL has the potential to improve performance on tasks with long-range dependencies. Extending this approach to more challenging datasets requires more expressive models and architectures capable of supporting computationally tractable RTRL. To address this requirement, the Linear Recurrent Unit (LRU) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orvieto et al., 2023</a>)</cite> is adopted for the following experiments. The LRU is a complex-valued linear RNN with element-wise recurrence, enabling computationally tractable RTRL by significantly reducing the size of the required influence matrix <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zucchet et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. By choosing the LRU, tPC RTRL can be scaled from the small tasks considered so far, to more complex, real-world datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">WikiText-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Merity et al., 2017</a>)</cite> is a word-level language modelling dataset consisting of high-quality English Wikipedia articles. The train split contains approximately 2,000,000 tokens across 600 distinct articles with a vocabulary size of 33,000 words. The validation and test splits each contain just over 200,000 tokens from 60 articles.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Setup:</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Before training, the vocabulary is reduced to the most frequent 10,000 words, all tokens are converted to lowercase, and markdown syntax is removed. The dataset is then split into chunks of 70 tokens. These tokens are embedded using frozen 300-dimension FastText <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bojanowski et al., 2017</a>)</cite> word embeddings. The embeddings are pretrained using Wikipedia data, and therefore, there is a minimal, but non-zero risk of information leakage from the training data into the WikiText-2 validation and test splits.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All models consist of a single LRU block with a recurrent state size of 1,024 and a hidden state size of 300, followed by 2 readout projections with dropout and <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">tanh</span> nonlinearities. The first projects to the hidden state size of 300, and the second projects to the vocabulary size of 10,000. This gives a total of 4,332,472 trainable parameters for each model. As in Section <a href="#S4.SS1" title="4.1 Copy Task ‣ 4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.1</span></a>, all BP-based models are trained with a cross-entropy loss, whilst the PC-based models use a squared-error loss function for internal energy and a cross-entropy loss function for output energy. Both PC models use an inference learning rate of 0.1 for 3 iterations. All models are trained with a batch size of 64, for 20 epochs. For a full description of the experimental setup, see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS2" title="D.2 WikiText-2 ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results:</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Results: ‣ 4.2 WikiText-2 ‣ 4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the mean test perplexity of the final trained models, averaged over 5 runs, with the epoch with the lowest validation loss used for evaluation. The baseline tPC and spatial BP methods perform worst, with mean perplexities of 108.99 and 103.38 respectively. BPTT and tPC RTRL achieve slightly lower mean perplexity of 98.62 and 99.19 respectively, indicating some performance gain from the ability to capture longer-range relationships. Even though all methods are close in performance, these results appear consistent with a two-tailed t-test yielding <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;0.01</annotation></semantics></math> for all comparisons between the models.</p>
</div>

</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ Results: ‣ 4.2 WikiText-2 ‣ 4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows the train and validation loss of each model over the course of training. Again, tPC RTRL appears to converge at a similar rate to BPTT. Although this provides evidence that tPC RTRL performs similarly to BPTT on this task, it is clear that there is minimal performance gain from the ability to model long-range relationships when performing next-token prediction at this scale. This phenomenon has been noted in other works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Menick et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. Section <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Machine Translation ‣ 4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a> aims to address this, exploring the application of tPC RTRL to a more complex dataset where the ability to capture these relationships is critical.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18131v1/data/wikitext_vert.png" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:673/573;" width="673" height="573" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Mean Train and Validation Loss During Training on WikiText-2 in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 WikiText-2 ‣ 4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, Averaged Over 5 Runs.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Machine Translation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To test the ability of tPC RTRL to scale to tasks with more complex long-range dependencies, a machine translation task is considered. In this task, models trained with limited temporal information typically struggle. This is because the entire source sentence must be consumed before outputting a translation, introducing a long-range dependency between corresponding tokens in the source and target sentences.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Setup:</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A translation task is constructed using a subset of the CCMatrix dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schwenk et al., 2021</a>)</cite>. This dataset contains 1.5 billion parallel sentence pairs across 200 languages. An English-French subset of 600,000 sentence pairs is sampled from the dataset, with 500,000 pairs used for training, 50,000 for validation and 50,000 for testing. During sampling, sentences are filtered to ensure a maximum total sequence length of 128 tokens. Minimal preprocessing is performed on the dataset, with all text converted to lowercase and tokenised using a Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) tokeniser <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sennrich et al., 2016</a>)</cite> trained on the source and target sentences from the training set. The vocabulary size is set to 10,000 tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The underlying models are the same architecture as those used in Section <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 WikiText-2 ‣ 4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a>, now with a recurrent state size of 1,024 and a hidden state size of 1,024 for a total of 15,498,000 trainable parameters. Both BP-based models use a cross-entropy loss, with 0.1 label smoothing applied to the target output. The PC models use squared-error loss functions for the internal energy and the same smoothed cross-entropy loss function for the output energy. The tPC RTRL model used an inference learning rate of 0.025 for 3 inference iterations, whilst the baseline tPC model used an inference learning rate of 0.01 for 5 iterations. All models are trained with a batch size of 128, for 20 epochs. For a full description of training setup, architectures and hyperparameters, see Appendix <a href="#A4.SS3" title="D.3 English-French Translation ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results:</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Results: ‣ 4.3 Machine Translation ‣ 4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the test perplexity and BLEU scores <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Papineni et al., 2002</a>)</cite> for all models on the reserved English-French translation set, showing that BPTT and tPC RTRL achieve low perplexities of 7.49 and 7.62 and BLEU scores of 21.11 and 20.71, respectively, substantially outperforming spatial BP and tPC. Translations were generated via beam search with a beam size of 10 and length penalty of 0.7, with these settings chosen by a validation sweep to optimise BLEU. Spatial BP and tPC not only have much higher perplexities, but also produce poorer translations with minimal overlap, as reflected in their poor BLEU scores. In the case of tPC, the model failed to converge to the level of spatial BP, even after extensive hyperparameter tuning.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">

</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Results: ‣ 4.3 Machine Translation ‣ 4 Experiments" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the train and validation loss of each model over the course of training, demonstrating that both tPC RTRL and BPTT appear to behave similarly, converging at an almost identical rate, and to similar final loss values. The alignment of quantitative metrics and training behaviour confirms that tPC RTRL effectively tackles this task in a manner similar to BPTT without sacrificing training stability.</p>
</div>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Discussion and Opportunities</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The experiments conducted in this work demonstrate that tPC RTRL provides a compelling method of conducting spatio-temporal credit assignment in RNNs without relying on BPTT. Results across a synthetic sequence copying task, WikiText-2, and an English-French translation task consistently show that tPC RTRL closely matches the performance of BPTT, overcoming the limitations of tPC. By retaining the local, parallelisable properties of its predecessors, tPC RTRL is a promising candidate for application on edge AI hardware, where the low-energy potential of this algorithm enable efficient online learning.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scaling and Hardware Considerations</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To train an RNN with BPTT, the unrolled computation graph must be held in memory, leading to memory requirements that scale linearly with sequence length. BPTT also suffers from both forward and backward locking, where layers must wait for others to finish before proceeding. This sequential behaviour limits spatial parallelism and makes BPTT poorly suited for neuromorphic deployment, where long-range communication and repeated transfers between global memory and compute are energetically unfavourable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">PC, and its temporal counterpart tPC, replace spatial BP with local inference and learning rules. The nature of these rules means they do not suffer from forward or backward locking and computation is dominated by operations that can be parallelised across the network. However, in its basic form, temporal credit assignment in tPC is limited, and performance on tasks with long-range dependencies is poor. tPC RTRL addresses this, improving temporal credit assignment without storing the full unrolled graph or restricting spatial parallelism. For a dense <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>-unit recurrent layer with <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>P</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P</annotation></semantics></math> recurrent parameters, RTRL requires <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(nP)\approx O(n^{3})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>P</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(nP)\approx O(n^{3})</annotation></semantics></math> memory and compute to maintain the influence matrix. However, using an element-wise recurrent unit, such as the LRU, diagonalises this matrix, reducing memory and compute required to maintain it to <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(P)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(P)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">From a hardware perspective, these algorithms naturally lend themselves to different paradigms. BPTT relies on global synchronisation and large, compute-heavy matrix operations, well-suited to GPUs. In contrast, tPC consists of more simple, local operations, enabling spatial parallelism and better matching hardware where compute and memory are distributed and co-located, such as near-memory neuromorphic systems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Davies et al., 2018</a>)</cite>. This locality minimises the need for global data movement, alleviating the von Neumman bottleneck and improving energy efficiency. However, this work has not yet explored the implementation of tPC RTRL on such platforms. Future efforts should bridge this gap, reporting real energy measurements is essential to validate the efficiency claims that underpin the field of PC. Such an implementation would be a significant step towards training RNNs on neuromorphic hardware capable of rivalling the performance of their BPTT, GPU-trained counterparts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Practical Considerations</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As with other PC-based methods, the choices of inference hyperparameters, such as the inference learning rate and number of iterations, influence convergence. For this work, a moderate amount of tuning was required to find suitable values for each task. However, in the large-scale translation task, no suitable hyperparameters were found for the baseline tPC model. This meant that it did not get near the level of the spatial BP model and highlights that further research is needed to better understand the nature of PC-based optimisation in neural networks. Years of experience with BP-based methods have led to a strong understanding of best practices, or “tips and tricks”, for training these models. This includes initialisation schemes <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Glorot and Bengio, 2010</a>)</cite>, normalisation techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ioffe and Szegedy, 2015</a>)</cite>, selection of activation functions, or architectural choices. However, PC lacks this level of understanding, making it difficult to apply in practice. In recent years, a number of works have begun to develop this area, helping to better robustly apply these techniques <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pinchetti et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frieder et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Frieder and Lukasiewicz, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Innocenti et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. This progress is orthogonal to the work in this paper and any advances are likely to benefit the presented tPC RTRL approach.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Architectural Extensions</h4>

<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All experiments in this work used architectures with a single recurrent layer as multi-layer RNNs require storing <math id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="O(L^{2})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">O(L^{2})</annotation></semantics></math> influence matrices or making layer-local approximations to keep memory scaling under control. While prior work suggests these layer-local assumptions recover some benefits of network depth <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zucchet et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, this has not yet been validated within the tPC RTRL framework. Future work should look to develop in this direction, demonstrating the potential of tPC RTRL to scale to deeper architectures.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Furthermore, although this work opted for the LRU to ensure RTRL remains computationally tractable, the algorithm could work with other element-wise recurrent units, such as the element-wise Long Short-Term Memory cell <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Irie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. Or alternatively, could use sparse and factorised approximations of RTRL to reduce the computational complexity and memory footprint of maintaining the influence matrices.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work introduced a novel extension to tPC, for the first time making use of RTRL to address critical shortcomings of existing approaches to PC in RNNs. The empirical evaluations presented demonstrate that tPC RTRL not only closely matches the performance of BPTT, but retains clear advantages such as local, parallelisable computation. These findings position tPC RTRL as a promising, biologically-inspired learning algorithm for RNNs which is particularly suited for deployment on edge AI platforms, representing a significant step towards low-power energy-efficient training of these networks. Further work will refine and scale this method. The continued exploration of tPC and RTRL aims to contribute towards a new generation of energy-efficient intelligent systems capable of learning complex temporal relationships from real-world data on next-generation hardware.</p>
</div>

<li id="bib.bib11" class="ltx_bibitem ltx_bib_inproceedings"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_bib_author-year ltx_role_refnum ltx_tag_bibitem">Irie <span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_etal">et al.</span> (2024)</span>

<p id="S6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Learning Long-Range Dependencies with Temporal Predictive Coding - Appendix</span></p>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Inference Learning Algorithm</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ Appendix A Inference Learning Algorithm" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> provides a full description of the Inference Learning (IL) algorithm for a discriminative PC network.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> IL for a discriminative PC network</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="alg1.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom"><span id="alg1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input</span>: Target output <math id="alg1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, input data <math id="alg1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{L}</annotation></semantics></math>, parameters <math id="alg1.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, inference iterations <math id="alg1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\text{iter}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>iter</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\text{iter}}</annotation></semantics></math>, inference learning rate <math id="alg1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>, and parameter learning rate <math id="alg1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math>.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="alg1.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Output:</span> Updated parameters.</p></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<div id="alg1.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_figure_panel ltx_listing">
<div id="alg1.l1" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">1:</span>
            
           Initialise latent variables <math id="alg1.l1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{1:L}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐱</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{1:L}</annotation></semantics></math> to feed-forward values.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l2" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">2:</span>
            
           <span id="alg1.l2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Inference (E-step)</span>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l3" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">3:</span>
            
           <span id="alg1.l3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <math id="alg1.l3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="alg1.l3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\text{iter}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>iter</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\text{iter}}</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>



</div>
<div id="alg1.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">4:</span>
            
            Compute <math id="alg1.l4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}=g_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{l+1};\mathbf{W}_{l})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}=g_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{l+1};\mathbf{W}_{l})</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l5" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">5:</span>
            
            Compute <math id="alg1.l5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{l}=\mathbf{x}_{l}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{l}=\mathbf{x}_{l}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l6" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">6:</span>
            
            Update <math id="alg1.l6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{l}\leftarrow\mathbf{x}_{l}-\alpha\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\mathbf{x}_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{l}\leftarrow\mathbf{x}_{l}-\alpha\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\mathbf{x}_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l7" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">7:</span>
            
           <span id="alg1.l7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l7.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l8" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">8:</span>
            
           <span id="alg1.l8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Learning (M-step)</span>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l9" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">9:</span>
            
           Update <math id="alg1.l9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{l}\leftarrow\mathbf{W}_{l}-\eta\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{l}\leftarrow\mathbf{W}_{l}-\eta\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg1.l10" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">10:</span>
            
           Return updated parameters <math id="alg1.l10.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
</div></div></div>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Temporal PC Algorithm</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Algorithm <a href="#alg2" title="Algorithm 2 ‣ Appendix B Temporal PC Algorithm" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> provides a full description of the Temporal PC (tPC) algorithm for a discriminative tPC network with multiple recurrent layers.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg2" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 2</span> </span> Learning with a tPC network</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="alg2.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom"><span id="alg2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input</span>: Sensory input <math id="alg2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{(t)}_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{(t)}_{0}</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="alg2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t\in{1,\ldots T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>∈</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t\in{1,\ldots T}</annotation></semantics></math>, parameters <math id="alg2.m3" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, inference iterations <math id="alg2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\text{iter}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>iter</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\text{iter}}</annotation></semantics></math>, inference learning rate <math id="alg2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>, and parameter learning rate <math id="alg2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math>.
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="alg2.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Output:</span> Updated parameters.</p></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<div id="alg2.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_figure_panel ltx_listing">
<div id="alg2.l1" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">1:</span>
            
           Initialise hidden state <math id="alg2.l1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1:L}^{(0)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{1:L}^{(0)}</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg2.l2" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">2:</span>
            
           <span id="alg2.l2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <math id="alg2.l2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="alg2.l2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg2.l2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>



</div>
<div id="alg2.l3" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">3:</span>

</div>
<div id="alg2.l5" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">5:</span>
            
             Compute <math id="alg2.l5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}=g_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{l+1}^{(t)},\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{l}^{(t-1)};\mathbf{W}_{l})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>𝐱</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}=g_{l}(\mathbf{x}_{l+1}^{(t)},\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{l}^{(t-1)};\mathbf{W}_{l})</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg2.l6" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">6:</span>
            
             Compute <math id="alg2.l6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{l}=\mathbf{x}_{l}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>𝝁</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{l}=\mathbf{x}_{l}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l}</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
<div id="alg2.l7" class="ltx_listingline">

             Update <math id="alg2.l7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{l}\leftarrow\mathbf{x}_{l}-\alpha\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\mathbf{x}_{l}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msub><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{l}\leftarrow\mathbf{x}_{l}-\alpha\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}}{\partial\mathbf{x}_{l}}</annotation></semantics></math>.

<div id="alg2.l16" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline">16:</span>
            
           Return updated parameters <math id="alg2.l16.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{0:L-1}</annotation></semantics></math>.

</div>
</div></div></div>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>tPC RTRL Algorithm</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The full algorithm for tPC RTRL is shown in Algorithm <a href="#alg3" title="Algorithm 3 ‣ Appendix C tPC RTRL Algorithm" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. This version of the algorithm uses time-batched updates, where parameter updates are accumulated across all time steps before being applied. However, the algorithm can be easily adapted to use immediate updates by moving the parameter update step inside the time loop.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Section <a href="#S5.SS0.SSS0.Px2" title="Practical Considerations ‣ 5 Discussion and Opportunities" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> briefly highlighted some of the works aiming to improve the practical application of PC-based methods. One such work, by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qi et al. (2025)</a></cite>, found that altering the error term used in the free energy during parameter updates improved training stability and convergence. In their formulation, the free energy is altered by changing the error term to:</p>
<table id="A3.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{l}^{(t)}=\mathbf{x}_{l}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l,0}^{(t)}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_mathvariant_bold-italic" mathvariant="bold-italic">ϵ</mi><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msubsup><mi>𝝁</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_{l}^{(t)}=\mathbf{x}_{l}^{(t)}-\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l,0}^{(t)},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l,0}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝝁</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\boldsymbol{\mu}_{l,0}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the initial guess for the latent variables at time <math id="A3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, defined by the feedforward initialisation. This change defines a corresponding learning-phase free energy, <math id="A3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}^{(t)}_{\mathbf{W}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}^{(t)}_{\mathbf{W}}</annotation></semantics></math>, whilst leaving the free energy used at inference unchanged. Altering the parameter updates in this way improved stability and end performance of both tPC and tPC RTRL and therefore was adopted for all experiments in this work.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg3" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 3</span> </span> tPC RTRL for a discriminative tPC network with a single recurrent layer and time-batched updates.</figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<p id="alg3.3" class="ltx_p ltx_figure_panel ltx_framed ltx_framed_topbottom"><span id="alg3.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Input</span>: Input data <math id="alg3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{L}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{L}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math>, target output <math id="alg3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{0}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{0}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math>, non-readout parameters <math id="alg3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{L-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{L-1}</annotation></semantics></math>, readout parameters <math id="alg3.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{0:L-2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>𝐖</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{0:L-2}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="alg3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\text{iter}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>iter</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\text{iter}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="alg3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>α</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="alg3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math>.
<span id="alg3.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Output:</span> Updated parameters.</p></div><div class="ltx_flex_break"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_1">
<div id="alg3.4" class="ltx_listing ltx_figure_panel ltx_listing">

</div>
<div id="alg3.l10" class="ltx_listingline">

</div>

alttext="\Delta\mathbf{W}_{L-1}=-\eta\left(\underbrace{\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}^{(t)}_{\mathbf{W}}}{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}}\frac{\partial\boldsymbol{\mu}^{(t)}}{\partial\hat{\mathbf{x}}^{(t-1)}}\mathbf{M}^{(t-1)}}_{\text{Historic}}+\underbrace{\frac{\partial\mathcal{F}^{(t)}_{\mathbf{W}}}{\partial\mathbf{W}^{(t)}_{L-1}}}_{\text{Immediate}}\right)" </section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Experimental Setup</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section will detail the experimental setup for all three tasks considered in this work. This includes the sequence copying task, language modelling on WikiText-2, and machine translation on an English-French subset of CCMatrix.</p>
</div>
<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Sequence Copying Task</h3>

<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The models used in the sequence copying task are all many-to-many RNNs with a single hidden layer and <span id="A4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">tanh</span> nonlinearities. In practice, this means that the hidden state and output at time <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> are computed as:</p>
<table id="A4.EGx11" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A4.E15"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{h}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{h}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E15.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\text{tanh}(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\mathbf{W}_{\textit{ih}}+\mathbf{h}^{(t-1)}\mathbf{W}_{\textit{hh}})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>tanh</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">ih</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">hh</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\text{tanh}(\mathbf{x}^{(t)}\mathbf{W}_{\textit{ih}}+\mathbf{h}^{(t-1)}\mathbf{W}_{\textit{hh}}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A4.E16"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathbf{y}_{\mu}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathbf{y}_{\mu}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.E16.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\mathbf{h}^{(t)}\mathbf{W}_{\textit{ho}}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">ho</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\mathbf{h}^{(t)}\mathbf{W}_{\textit{ho}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\textit{ih}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">ih</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\textit{ih}}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\textit{hh}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">hh</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\textit{hh}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{\textit{ho}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">ho</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{\textit{ho}}</annotation></semantics></math> are the input, hidden and output weight matrices respectively. <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐱</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the input at time <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the hidden state at time <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}_{\mu}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}_{\mu}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> is the predicted output at time <math id="A4.SS1.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The BP-based approaches all used a cross-entropy loss function and then, for any incoming loss, either unrolled the network across all time steps (BPTT) or detached the compute graph at the current time step (spatial BP). The tPC model used a squared-error loss function for internal energy and a cross-entropy loss function for output energy. This gives a total energy function of:</p>
<table id="A4.E17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A4.E17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{F}^{(t)}=||\mathbf{h}^{(t)}_{\mu}-\mathbf{h}^{(t)}||^{2}+\textit{CE}({\mathbf{y}}_{\mu}^{(t)},\mathbf{y}^{(t)})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℱ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">CE</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>𝐲</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{F}^{(t)}=||\mathbf{h}^{(t)}_{\mu}-\mathbf{h}^{(t)}||^{2}+\textit{CE}({\mathbf{y}}_{\mu}^{(t)},\mathbf{y}^{(t)}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(17)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Here, the subscript <math id="A4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> is used to differentiate between the predicted variables and their free or clamped counterparts. The networks are then trained using either tPC or tPC RTRL.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ D.1 Sequence Copying Task ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> provides a summary of the hyperparameters used in this task for all models, including the hyperparameter search which was conducted to find them. All models were trained using the Adam optimiser <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kingma and Ba, 2015</a>)</cite> with no learning rate schedule.</p>
</div>

<td id="A4.T4.1.11.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">-</td>
<td id="A4.T4.1.11.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">-</td>
<td id="A4.T4.1.11.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">[0, 0.9]</td>
<td id="A4.T4.1.11.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">0.9</td>
<td id="A4.T4.1.11.7" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb">0.9</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>Hyperparameter values and search ranges used for the sequence copying task. If a range is specified, the optimal values shown are the best performing hyperparameters found during an exhaustive grid search.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.2 </span>WikiText-2</h3>

<div id="A4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">All models used for the WikiText-2 task are LRUs with a 2-layer readout head. The hidden state, intermediate states, and output at time <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> are computed as:</p>
<table id="A4.EGx12" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(21)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐁</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{B}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐂</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{C}</annotation></semantics></math> are complex-valued weight matrices, <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝐃</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{D}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{r}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{r}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{W}_{o}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝐖</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{W}_{o}</annotation></semantics></math> are a real-valued weight matrices. The vectors <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> are complex-valued vectors used for element-wise multiplication, denoted by <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\odot" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\odot</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> is a binary dropout mask. When this work refers to the recurrent state size of the LRU, it refers to the size of the complex-valued variable <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{h}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{h}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math>, when it refers to the hidden state size, it refers to the size of <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{\textit{lru}}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">lru</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{\textit{lru}}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A4.SS2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{x}_{\textit{r}}^{(t)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>𝐱</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_italic">r</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{x}_{\textit{r}}^{(t)}</annotation></semantics></math>. For a full description of the LRU, see <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Orvieto et al. (2023)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A free energy, defined over this architecture, is computed as:</p>

<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A4.Ex5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}||Re[\mathbf{h}^{(t)}_{\mu}]-Re[\mathbf{h}^{(t)}]||^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msubsup><mi>𝐡</mi><mi>μ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msup><mi>𝐡</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}||Re[\mathbf{h}^{(t)}_{\mu}]-Re[\mathbf{h}^{(t)}]||^{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(22)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A4.SS2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">with the subscript <math id="A4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mu" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>μ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mu</annotation></semantics></math> used to differentiate between the predicted variables and their free or clamped counterparts. The first two terms are the squared error of the real and imaginary parts of the hidden state, the third term is the squared error of the LRU output, the fourth term is the squared error of the readout intermediate layer, and the final term is a cross-entropy loss function applied to the readout output.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Unlike with the sequence copying task, it was not feasible to perform an exhaustive hyperparameter search for the PC-based moels on this dataset. Instead, the hyperparameters are tuned by hand, attempting to find a balance between end performance and stability. The hyperparameters used for the WikiText-2 task are shown in Table <a href="#A4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ D.2 WikiText-2 ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>. All models were trained using the Adam optimiser with a cosine learning rate schedule with a warmup period lasting for 10% of the total training steps.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.T5" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A4.T5.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A4.T5.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A4.T5.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_border_tt"></td>
<td id="A4.T5.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" colspan="2"><span id="A4.T5.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BP</span></td>

<section id="A4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.3 </span>English-French Translation</h3>

<div id="A4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The architecture for the translation task is the same as that used for WikiText-2, with the exception that the recurrent state size and hidden state size are both set to 1,024. The free energy is computed in the same way as for WikiText-2, with the addition of label smoothing applied to the cross-entropy loss function used for the output energy. This is done to improve generalisation and reduce overfitting. The hyperparameters used for this task are shown in Table <a href="#A4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ D.3 English-French Translation ‣ Appendix D Experimental Setup" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>. As with WikiText-2, these hyperparameters were tuned by hand. All models were trained using the Adam optimiser with a cosine learning rate schedule with a warmup period lasting for 10% of the total training steps.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The embedding layer used to embed the BPE tokenised input is trained from scratch with BPTT on an independent training run which is not used for evaluation throughout this work. It is then kept frozen for all training runs.</p>
</div>

        <span style="position: relative; bottom: -0.4ex;">E</span>
      </span>
      <span class="ltx_font_smallcaps">xml</span>
      <img alt="[LOGO]"
        src="data:image/png;base64,">
    </a>.
  </div>
  <div class="keyboard-glossary">
    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">
            <path
              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
  </div>
